claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by local atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity.
Deliberate compositional non-uniformity will lower the premelting transition relative to compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
Deliberate compositional non-uniformity will broaden the premelting transition relative to compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
Compositional inhomogeneity produces local variations in atomic bonding and cohesive energy, particularly at surfaces and grain boundaries.
Localized chemical heterogeneity creates zones of reduced cohesive energy.
Zones of reduced cohesive energy lower the energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
A lower atomic-diffusion barrier initiates premelting at a lower temperature than in a homogeneous nanoparticle.
Localized premelting changes propagate through the nanoparticle and affect the overall melting process.
Increasing chemical heterogeneity will cause an earlier onset of premelting relative to a uniformly mixed baseline.
Increasing chemical heterogeneity will lower the overall melting temperature relative to a uniformly mixed baseline.
Melting behavior will shift systematically with the degree of induced compositional gradient.
The proposed relationship should hold for multielement nanoparticles approximately 2–50 nm in size.
The proposed relationship should hold for HEA compositions that remain single-phase solid solutions under the test conditions.
